reason: Survived, though on thinner ground than the Adams line. The sentence is real and is the hinge of the vale of Soul-making passage. Two independent sources give it in exactly this capitalisation, “a World of Pains and troubles” and “an Intelligence” against a lowercase “soul”: the Mapping Keats's Progress project at the University of Victoria, and a transcription that names the edition as The Letters of John Keats: A New Selection, ed. Robert Gittings, Oxford University Press, 1970, pp. 248 to 251. Locator holds: the journal letter to George and Georgiana Keats in America runs 14 February to 3 May 1819 and the soul-making entry is that of 21 April 1819, which the Victoria chronology dates independently. Attribution holds and no trap in the misattribution list touches it. Scope holds: a letter of 1819, tagged Correspondence, which is the form of the work. It ends in a question mark, which the rules allow. It is publishable and it is a trial line, which is the month. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Keats stands at one of three for the year with month 4 only, so July does not double him. Source line leads with the name, no dash, no straight quote, 119 characters. What I could not close, and why it is not enough to refute: I never opened Gittings's volume, so the claim that Gittings specifically prints this capitalisation rests on one transcription that cites him plus one project page that does not name its edition, and Keats's capitals do vary between editors. One web summary offered the inverted form, lowercase world and intelligence against a capital Soul, but it produced no edition or page behind it and I treat an unsourced summary as no evidence. The same transcription also heads the letter 14 February to 8 May 1819, which is wrong against the standard 3 May and is the transcriber's slip, not the verifier's. If the assembler wants this airtight, the cheap fix is to read p. 250 of the Gittings selection or Rollins vol. 2 p. 102 and confirm the three capitals before it ships.
